result.summary: The poet opens a short hymn by announcing he will sing of Demeter and her daughter Persephone. He greets the goddess and asks her to protect the city and guide his song.

scenes.title: Invocation of Demeter
scenes.summary: The singer announces his subject, Demeter and Persephone, then hails the goddess and prays for the city's safety and for help with his song.

characters.name: Demeter
characters.description: rich-haired, awful goddess addressed by the singer

analysis.text: The hymn follows the usual pattern of a Homeric Hymn: naming the deity, praising her, greeting her and asking for her favor. Pairing mother and daughter points to their close bond in myth.
The request to keep the city safe shows that the hymn was performed in a civic or religious setting, where a community looked to Demeter for protection and prosperity.

fun_facts.text: This is one of the shortest Homeric Hymns, only three lines long, and is a brief prelude rather than a full narrative like the longer Hymn to Demeter.

language_notes.text: "Awful" here means inspiring awe and reverence, not terrible or bad.
"Govern my song" means guide or direct the poem, asking the goddess to inspire and control how the singer performs it.

context_notes.text: Demeter is the goddess of grain and harvest. Persephone, her daughter, was carried off to the underworld, which is the story this hymn goes on to tell.
Hymns often end the opening with a prayer for the local city, showing the singer performed for a community, probably at a festival.

literary_notes.text: "Rich-haired" is a fixed descriptive title for Demeter, typical of oral epic and hymn style, and "lovely" does similar work for Persephone.
The singer turns from narrating to address the goddess directly, creating a moment of ritual greeting.
